Subject: Follow-up: latency & context requirements (EdgeScale chat)

Rafael — thanks again for the call earlier. A quick recap and a few clarifying questions so we can compare options internally: 

- Our product: document-assisted conversational UI for customer support (real-time).
- Target SLOs: p50 first-token < 200ms, p95 first-token < 450ms for streaming responses; end-to-end latency target for a full exchange ~< 600ms where possible.
- Traffic baseline: expected steady-state concurrency ~80 active sessions, peak concurrency 200; average request mix ~40% long-context (20k-40k tokens input), 60% shorter (<=2k).
- Throughput: sustained ~150 reqs/sec, spiky bursts (short windows) up to 350 rps.
- Desired behavior on large contexts: prefer graceful fallbacks. Options we’re evaluating: 1) truncation (drop older context), 2) chunk+stitch (break into chunks, synthesize), 3) retrieval-only summarization (external RAG pre-processing), or 4) dedicated large-context model.

Specific asks from us after the call: 
1) Can Redwood meet the first-token streaming SLOs above for models that ingest 20k–40k input tokens? If not, what are realistic latency bands per token-window?
2) What are recommended fallback patterns you’ve implemented for apps like ours to preserve coherence?
3) Rough monthly cost ballpark for hosted vs. dedicated for our estimated 150rps steady (assume 60% short, 40% long).
4) Any constraints around concurrency ceilings, KV cache sizing, or steady-state batching we should design for?

Attaching a high-level product-arch diagram (product-arch.png). Happy to jump back on a call if helpful — Tom and I are available Fri afternoon PT.

Thanks,
Anya Patel

Anya — thanks for the clear recap and the diagram, very helpful. Below is a concise answer + proposed plan so you can share internally. I split answers into latency/throughput tradeoffs, recommended fallbacks, and a practical rollout path.

1) Can Redwood meet the streaming SLOs for 20k–40k inputs?
- Short answer: With our streaming execution path + continuous KV caching, we can hit p50 first-token ~160–240ms and p95 first-token ~350–550ms for the 20k window on our Dedicated / Private deployments; hosted performance depends on model selection and instance class but is comparable on higher tiers.
- Notes: the heavy cost is KV propagation and memory-bound attention when the full attention window is used. For 40k inputs you should expect p95 to be closer to 500–750ms unless you choose a large-context-optimized model (we offer variants).

2) Recommended fallbacks (practical, ordered by how often we see them used):
- Primary: Retrieval + dynamic prefixing — keep most recent N tokens in context, fetch relevant external docs via RAG, and prepend concise retrieved context. This saves tokens and preserves relevance.
- Secondary: Chunk-and-stitch for long historical context (server-side): break the long context into overlapping chunks, run multi-pass summaries, then synthesize a final prompt. Works well for long histories but adds complexity and some added latency at request time (we usually precompute summaries asynchronously).
- Tertiary: Graceful truncation + user-visible hint — truncate the oldest conversational turns and surface a short notice ("earlier messages omitted"). Fastest but can lose long-range coherence.
- Fallback switching: Redwood can automatically route to a compatible model variant (lower precision or larger memory VM) when the request exceeds the pinned model’s feasible window — this preserves availability at higher cost.

3) Concurrency/throughput constraints and engineering knobs:
- Concurrency: our Dedicated pods can sustain the 150 rps steady with 80 concurrent sessions if autoscaling and batching are configured; peak bursts to 350 rps are handled by burst capacity but will increase p95 latency during the burst.
- KV cache sizing: plan for KV cache per-session proportional to active context size; for 20k–40k contexts we often allocate 6–12GB/session for large-context models (varies by model/quantization).
- Batching: continuous batching reduces token-unit cost but increases first-token latency slightly — for your p50-first-token target, set max_batch_wait <= 6ms.

4) Cost and deployment guidance (ballpark):
- Hosted (managed API): ~$0.35–0.75 per 1k tokens for long-context flows depending on model; with your traffic (40% long) rough monthly bill ~ $35k–$70k.
- Dedicated (reserved capacity): depends on committed GPU pool; ballpark monthly (committed) for predictable 150rps with headroom: $25k–$50k + infra (savings vs. hosted at high sustained usage).
- Note: quantization and smaller model variants can dramatically lower the cost with modest accuracy tradeoffs.

Proposed next steps (mutual action plan):
- I. 48-hour canary on a dedicated pool: 50 qps, mixed short/long traffic — measure p50/p95 first-token, end-to-end, and per-token tail. (Action: Redwood ops — deliver pool + test harness)
- II. Parallel RAG experiment: run retrieval + dynamic prefixing for long-context subset (Action: EdgeScale engineering to supply retrieval index + sample queries)
- III. Post-canary review: decide hosting vs. dedicated and an initial commitment level (Action: 3-way review).

I attached a quick decision grid (SLO-deploy-options.xlsx) that summarizes options and rough costs. I’ve CC’d Ben (SRE/Perf) and Laura (Solutions) to help scope the canary and the RAG experiment. If Friday afternoon PT works, I can block 30–45 minutes to walk through the decision grid and the canary plan.

Thanks — Rafael

Anya — quick note on the questions above. Rafael covered the architecture and fallbacks well; a couple of extra data points for your finance/engineering teams: 

- Stitching guidance: we recommend 10–20% overlap between chunks with a dedicated summarization pass per chunk and a final synthesis prompt. In our tests this reduced hallucination by ~35% vs. naive concatenation.
- Cost table: I’ll paste a short ballpark you can copy to finance (monthly USD):
